rendered:
The premise is not what the paper says. It does not conclude that aqueous processing is incompatible with Ni-rich NMC 811[1]. Its conclusion is the opposite: "Overall, this work clearly demonstrates that aqueous processing is compatible with Ni-rich NMC 811[2]."

On the leaching data, the paper says that the percentage of leached Li+ rises with nickel content, but that even Ni-rich NMC 811[3] shows only minimal leaching, "leaching (~3 wt%) after one week[4]." XRD and Raman analysis after water exposure found that there were confirmed that there are no bulk structural[5] changes, and XPS showed only minor surface changes. Aqueous-processed pouch cells retained capacity slightly less well than NMP-processed cells (~70% vs. ~76%)[6], and the authors say the aqueous cells "the aqueous-processed NMC 811 cells still demonstrate very good cycling[7]."

The paper does flag real problems. "The main issue associated with processing NMC 811 in water is[8] Li+/H+ exchange, which raises the solution pH; a high pH "can corrode the aluminum foil current collector[9]." These issues arise "processing if formulation chemistry is not handled properly[10]. The authors expect them to be solved through formulation, mixing and formation-protocol optimization, and they suggest phosphoric acid additions as a possible fix. So the lithium leaching is treated as a manageable issue, not a reason to reject aqueous processing of Ni-rich cathodes.
